title: Birth and boyhood in the Irish Channel
summary: Born March 1909 near 7th and St. Thomas; Irish and Black neighbours looked after each other's children yet boys fought across ward lines.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Because everyone has called you Henry. Do you mind telling us when you were born and where, what part of the city and so on?
I was born on March 2, 1909. And we... Right here in New Orleans? In New Orleans, yes. In the area of the Irish Channel.
Around 7th, between St. Thomas and Chippewa.
Oh, yes. I know about where that is. I know St. Thomas and 7th. It was down between the river and Magazine, is that right? That's right. It really was the Irish Channel then, wasn't it?

Do you remember anything about your childhood? Did you live there long with... I've heard a lot of tales about how it was sort of a tough section of the Irish people down there and all. Well... Did you remember much of those times?

I can remember quite a bit of it. During that time there was quite an association between the Irish and the Negroes who lived in the area. The parents would have their children to remain if they went in town to do shopping. They would have their children to remain with either. If one of the Irish people had to go, they would ask my mother to keep their children and my mother would do the same by them. Now, during those times particularly, the boys didn't appreciate other boys visiting from other neighborhoods. If someone came from the 10th Ward into the 11th Ward, the whites and colors would fight together. And if they came in from either ward, they would always fight. Even if we would attempt to visit and other was, we too would have to fight.
Now, they would get angry with us many times if we wouldn't fight with them and would fight us. But it was all over again. We would play sandlot ball and it would be completed as such.
